method: PubMed E-utilities searches; every cited record's abstract was fetched in this session. Findings rest on abstracts; full texts were not read. Where evidence comes from another sport (mostly soccer), the finding says so.

demands.finding: College GPS data show practice workload intensity is driven mostly by drill type and day of the week rather than position alone, but each position group responds differently to each drill type, so conditioning needs to be planned per position and per drill (college, Division I).

In college players, maximal strength (back squat, hang clean) feeds change-of-direction ability through jump power in skill positions, while in linemen and other non-skill positions the hang clean relates to change of direction directly; strength alone does not explain agility (college).

Across elite team sports, American football was the only sport in a systematic review where high-intensity accelerations outnumbered decelerations; most other field sports are deceleration-dominant. Training for football should emphasise repeated short explosive starts.

College players' GPS player load tracked their repetitive head impact exposure within sessions and across a season, and both were higher in games than in practices; physical load may act as a rough proxy for head-impact exposure (college).

Exertional heat stroke deaths in football cluster around high-intensity conditioning that is not position-specific, exercise used as punishment, and failure to modify activity for heat and humidity; linemen need position-specific work-to-rest ratios (registry of youth, high school and college cases; NATA task force consensus).

High schools in states with mandated preseason heat-acclimatisation guidelines had roughly half the rate of exertional heat illness during preseason (adjusted rate ratio about 0.45, CI 0.23-0.87) (high school).

Only about a quarter of high schools reported using all six recommended exertional heat-stroke preparedness strategies; use was highest in hot regions with state mandates (high school athletic trainers survey).

injuries.finding: Among boys' high school contact and collision sports, football had the highest overall injury rate (3.87 per 1000 athlete-exposures), the highest severe injury rate (0.80/1000 AE) and the highest concussion risk; competition was about 4 times riskier than practice. The head/face was the most common site overall and the knee the most common site for severe injuries (high school, RIO surveillance).

Emergency-department presentations for football injuries were about 16 per 1000 high school participants per year and 12 per 1000 youth players, and both fell between 2010 and 2019; high schoolers were about twice as likely as youth players to present with knee injuries and 2.4 times as likely with shoulder injuries (youth and high school, NEISS).

Using identical methods across seven youth sports at one English high school, American football had the highest match injury incidence (86 per 1000 match-hours); concussion was the most common injury and 59% of injuries came from player contact (high school, age about 17-18).

In high school football, acromioclavicular sprains were the most common shoulder/arm/elbow injury, fractures cost the most time (about 42 days), about a third of these injuries came from tackling, and running backs and linebackers were most affected (high school, NATION-SP).

In NCAA football, shoulder and elbow injuries occurred at 13.2 per 10,000 exposures; AC separation was most common (30%) and instability episodes made up 28% of these injuries; tackling caused about 38% (college, NCAA ISP).

Boys' football had the second-highest ACL injury rate of any adolescent sport after girls' soccer (about 0.10 per 1000 athlete-exposures), and ACL injuries were about 7 times more likely in games than practice for boys (adolescent, systematic review).
A later adolescent meta-analysis put the per-season ACL risk for boys highest in football (0.82% per season), then lacrosse, and found club sport participation raised risk (adolescent).

Older youth athletes, girls, and those with prior concussion carried higher concussion risk (prior concussion 3-5 times); in this youth cohort football position did not change concussion risk (youth, baseline-testing cohort).
Shoulder dislocations in high school and college athletes presenting to EDs were 87% male, and football was the second-commonest sport after basketball (high school and college, NEISS).

differences.finding: Linemen carry the highest exertional heat-stroke risk; conditioning for linemen should use position-specific work-to-rest ratios and avoid high-intensity aerobic testing during transition periods.
For non-skill positions, the hang clean related directly to change-of-direction performance rather than through jump power, suggesting strength transfer differs from skill positions (college).
Running backs and linebackers had the largest share of shoulder, upper-arm and elbow injuries in high school football, about 15% each, largely from tackling.
In skill positions, maximal strength improved change of direction through better vertical jump power, so jump and power work is the link between the weight room and agility (college).
Position did not differ in concussion risk in a large youth cohort, and in college players position affected physical load but not head impact exposure.

riskReduction.finding: Limiting full contact in practice was associated with a 64% lower practice concussion rate in American football (systematic review of prevention strategies).
Mouthguards were associated with about a 26% lower concussion rate across collision sports.
Programmes that include the Nordic hamstring exercise roughly halve hamstring injury rates across sports; most trials are in soccer, so application to football is an extrapolation.
riskReduction.dose: varies by trial; see cross-cutting Nordic entries

riskReduction.finding: Neuromuscular training (landing, strength, balance) reduces ACL injuries by about half in all athletes; evidence for male athletes alone is insufficient, so for football it is a reasonable but not proven transfer.
riskReduction.effect: OR about 0.50 for all ACL injuries

riskReduction.finding: Heat acclimatisation policies following NATA-IATF guidance in the preseason were associated with fewer exertional heat illnesses.
exercises: phased preseason acclimatisation (equipment and session progression)
riskReduction.dose: per NATA-IATF guidance (details not in abstract)

riskReduction.finding: Padded helmet covers (Guardian Cap) reduced lab brain-injury metrics by 10-25% depending on speed, but on-field data in college linebackers showed no clear reduction; in the NFL their mandated use in preseason practice coincided with a 54-62% fall in concussions, though not for helmet-shell impacts specifically. Evidence is mixed and not from high school.

warmup.finding: No football-specific structured warm-up trial was found in this search; the best evidence is from youth team-sport neuromuscular programmes, which cut lower-extremity injuries by about a third (see cross-cutting).

adolescent.finding: High school football players who returned to play after arthroscopic shoulder stabilisation had a 16.7% recurrence rate, rising with years of eligibility remaining (42% in the youngest group); 60% chose not to return, mostly from fear of reinjury (age 14-17).

Only about two-thirds (67%) of football players returned to play after ACL reconstruction, at an average of about 11.6 months, and most performed below their pre-injury level (mixed high school, college and NFL, systematic review).
Injury rates were higher in competition than practice for high school football players, which points to managing game exposure and game-intensity practice periods.

demands.finding: In elite rugby union, backs cover more total and high-speed distance in training and matches, while forwards make far more tackles, tackle assists, breakdown entries and contact events (elite adult).

During ball-in-play periods, backs show higher metabolic and high-speed demands and forwards perform more collisions, and both running and collision demands change with the length of the passage of play (international adult).

In elite under-20 players, centres covered the most distance (about 6.5 km) and the front row the least (about 5.0 km); the back three did the most high-speed running and forwards carried greater contact loads (U20 elite).

injuries.finding: Youth rugby union match injury rates were about 40 per 1000 match-hours for boys and 69 for girls; concussion rates were about 6 per 1000 player-hours for boys and 34 for girls; the tackle caused most match injuries (55% boys, 71% girls); boys mostly injured the lower limb and girls the head/neck (youth, systematic review).
Senior amateur rugby union match injuries were about 47 per 1000 player-hours, mostly in contact, with the tackler at more risk than the ball-carrier (adult amateur, meta-analysis).

Irish schoolboy rugby had shoulder injuries at 12.2 per 1000 match-hours, higher than adult levels; dislocations/subluxations (34%) and AC sprains (30%) dominated, 81% came from the tackle, and forwards had about twice the shoulder injury rate of backs (schoolboy, cohort).

In elite Super Rugby, shoulder injuries occurred at 13 per 1000 player-hours, tacklers were hurt more than ball-carriers, and the two main mechanisms were landing on the ground with the arm across the body and internally rotated, and a direct blow to the side of the shoulder with the arm at the side (elite adult).

In elite tackles, most concussions happen to the tackler (77%); head-to-hip and head-to-knee contact are especially risky for the tackler, while head-to-head contact is worst for the ball-carrier; lower tackles protect the ball-carrier (elite adult, case-control video).

Rugby league match injury incidence varies by level and the hooker had the highest pooled incidence; head and neck injuries rose about 10-fold compared with the 2014 analysis (all levels, systematic review).
Rugby union hamstring injury risk factors include position, fatigue, previous injury and between-leg strength imbalance (systematic review, mixed levels).

differences.finding: Forwards do far more collisions and contact actions and, in schoolboys, about twice the shoulder injury rate of backs; forwards are also stronger in the hamstrings than backs.
Backs cover greater total and high-speed distances and have higher metabolic load, so their conditioning should emphasise repeated high-speed running.
The hooker had the highest pooled match injury incidence of any rugby league position.

riskReduction.finding: A pre-activity movement control programme (the RFU 'Activate' programme) in schoolboys aged 14-18 cut concussion and match injuries; when teams did it at least three times a week, overall match injuries fell by about 72% and concussions by about 59%.
exercises: neck exercises in the programme (per trial design)
riskReduction.dose: pre-activity warm-up, at least 3 sessions per week for full effect
riskReduction.effect: ITT: concussion RR 0.71; teams with 3+ weekly sessions: match injuries RR 0.28, concussion RR 0.41

riskReduction.finding: The same movement control programme in adult community rugby gave likely reductions of 40% in lower-limb injuries and 60% in concussion, with larger effects in high-compliance clubs.
riskReduction.dose: before training and matches; higher compliance mattered

riskReduction.finding: Neck-strengthening programmes reduced concussion in male rugby players by about 45% in the two studies that measured it; no evidence yet for female rugby players or soccer.
exercises: cervical strengthening (isometric and resisted neck work)

riskReduction.finding: Weak neck extensors (under about 36 kg) and left-right asymmetry in neck side-flexion strength were linked to much higher odds of missing games from head, neck and face injuries in pro rugby league.
exercises: neck extension and lateral flexion strengthening (modifiable target)
riskReduction.effect: OR about 8 for weak extensors, about 12.6 for asymmetry (exploratory)

riskReduction.finding: Progressive Nordic programmes increased hamstring strength and muscle thickness and reduced imbalance in rugby players, and reduced injury incidence and severity in professionals.
riskReduction.effect: reduced incidence and severity in pros

riskReduction.finding: Lowering the legal tackle height to the armpit in amateur rugby showed a non-significant trend toward fewer concussions; most head injuries still happened in the tackle.

warmup.finding: In high school girls' rugby, a neuromuscular warm-up did not significantly change match injury or concussion rates, but head-injury burden (days lost) was lower in intervention seasons; concussions were 31-41% of all match injuries (high school girls).
The youth rugby systematic review found neuromuscular training to be the most promising prevention strategy, though only eight studies tested any prevention.

adolescent.finding: In youth rugby, higher playing level and older age were the risk factors with the strongest evidence.
Neck strength rises with age and is higher in males; adolescent male rugby players with a history of concussion had a lower neck flexor-to-extensor strength ratio (adolescent to adult).

Female university players had 47% lower isometric neck strength than males and showed uncontrolled whiplash in most head-impact events, so male-derived neck and tackle protocols may not transfer to girls (university).

demands.finding: Successful wrestlers across ages, weight classes and styles have high anaerobic power and capacity, good aerobic fitness for recovery between periods, and high maximal, isometric, explosive and strength-endurance; flexibility did not separate successful from less successful wrestlers (review).

Rapid weight loss ('cutting weight') by dehydration and food restriction is common; losing more than about 5% of body mass quickly is linked to worse performance, more injury, lower testosterone, higher cortisol and higher eating-disorder risk (narrative review, includes female wrestlers).
A decision-tree approach to acute weight loss in combat sports aims to minimise performance loss; chronic body-fat reduction is preferred to large acute manipulations (review, Olympic combat sports).

injuries.finding: High school boys' wrestling injury rate was 2.38 per 1000 athlete-exposures versus 9.28 in college; in high school the head/face and shoulder/clavicle were the most common sites, while college wrestlers most often injured the knee (high school RIO and NCAA ISP).
Wrestling-related concussions and closed head injuries seen in EDs peak at ages 15-16 and are 96% male; wrestlers may under-report symptoms as normal fatigue (NEISS).

Among high school wrestlers with concussion, two-thirds occurred in competition, takedowns were the most common player mechanism (59%) and head-to-mat/wall the most common contact mechanism (56%) (high school, cohort).
Head and face injuries from wrestling seen in EDs were mostly under age 18 (82%); concussion was the commonest diagnosis and the takedown the commonest mechanism (NEISS).
In youth athletes, wrestling and martial arts had the highest relative concussion risk of all sports compared (youth).
In college wrestling, knee injuries were mostly ligament (53%) and meniscus (22%); about a fifth of wrestlers had a recurrent knee injury (college, cohort).
Skin fungal infection (tinea corporis gladiatorum) spreads by repeated skin contact among wrestlers; mat and skin hygiene matter (review).

differences.finding: Anaerobic power and capacity distinguish successful wrestlers regardless of weight class; the main weight-class-specific risk is weight cutting, which is worse when losses exceed about 5% of body mass.

riskReduction.finding: Takedowns and head-to-mat contact drive concussion, so safe-fall and takedown technique, and neck strength (see cross-cutting), are the logical targets; no wrestling-specific prevention trial was found in this search.
Avoiding rapid weight loss of more than about 5% body mass protects performance and health; plan weight class through gradual body-fat change.

warmup.finding: No wrestling-specific structured warm-up trial was found; the youth team-sport neuromuscular training evidence (about one-third fewer lower-extremity injuries) is the nearest guide.

adolescent.finding: Head injuries in wrestling are concentrated in 15-16 year olds, the high school years, so concussion education and symptom reporting should target that age group.
High school wrestlers have a lower total injury rate than college wrestlers but more head/face and shoulder injuries proportionally.

demands.finding: Hockey is repeated bursts of fast skating with sharp changes in speed and direction and frequent contact, in shifts of about 30-80 seconds totalling about 15-25 minutes on ice; nearly half the distance is at high intensity, forwards more than defence; both phosphagen and glycolytic energy and a strong aerobic base matter, and skating ability fades late in games, linked to glycogen depletion (review).

injuries.finding: In a 5-year Canadian cohort of 4418 players aged 11-17, game injury risk was higher in girls (IRR 1.57), those with a previous injury (1.46) and those with a concussion history (1.41); goaltenders had about half the injury rate of forwards (youth).
Body checking brings a 2-3 times higher risk of all injury, severe injury and concussion at all levels of boys' youth hockey (AAP policy statement).

Injuries happen much more in games than practices and risk rises with each level of play; mandatory facial protection and delaying body checking until age 13 are proven protections (review across levels).
In US data, eliminating body checking at Pee Wee cut overall injuries by about 17% and checking-related injuries by 38%, though reported concussions rose in that dataset (youth registry).

differences.finding: Goaltenders had about half the injury rate of forwards in youth hockey.

Elite goalies reach near end-range hip internal rotation, most extremely when decelerating on skates rather than in the butterfly itself; repetitive end-range internal rotation is the likely driver of hip impingement (FAI) in goalies (elite).
Goalies using the butterfly put the hip in flexion with end-range internal rotation, a position linked to overuse hip and labral injury; rehabilitation must progress on ice (clinical commentary).
Forwards show a more intense activity pattern than defence.

riskReduction.finding: Disallowing body checking in 11-12 year old (Pee Wee) leagues halved game injuries and cut concussions by 64%.
exercises: policy: no body checking under age 13

riskReduction.finding: Across child and adolescent hockey, no-checking policies were associated with 58% fewer concussions, with no unintended rise in other injuries.
The no-checking policy for 11-12 year olds was also likely cost-saving for health care.
riskReduction.effect: about 2.2 fewer game injuries per 1000 player-hours

riskReduction.finding: A preseason adductor strengthening programme in pro players identified as weak cut adductor strains from 3.2 to 0.71 per 1000 game exposures.
riskReduction.dose: 6 weeks preseason for players screened as at-risk

riskReduction.finding: Screening the hip adductor-to-abductor strength ratio preseason and in season can flag hockey players at risk of groin strain who would benefit from strengthening (level 3 evidence).

warmup.finding: No hockey-specific injury-prevention warm-up trial was returned in this search; youth team-sport neuromuscular evidence is the nearest guide.

adolescent.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends restricting body checking to elite boys' levels and starting no earlier than age 15, and expanding non-checking programmes.
Girls' hockey players had higher game and practice injury risk than boys in the Canadian cohort, even though girls' hockey does not allow checking.

demands.finding: In elite men's international lacrosse, attack and defence players covered more total distance and more low-intensity accelerations and decelerations, while midfielders had the highest average speed and sprint distance; midfielders should emphasise anaerobic power (elite adult).

injuries.finding: Across lacrosse studies, the lower leg, ankle and foot had the highest injury rate (0.66 per 1000 athlete-exposures) for both sexes, with no significant sex difference in rates by body region (systematic review, mixed levels).

Among 11-18 year olds treated in EDs, boys were 1.6 times more likely to be hurt by player contact and girls 2.2 times more likely to have non-contact injuries; stick injuries fall and player contact rises with age (youth, NEISS).

Boys' club summer lacrosse had an injury rate of 2.13 per 1000 exposures, similar to high school football and wrestling; head/face was the commonest site (22%), concussions were 19% of injuries, and midfielders were injured most (41%) (youth club).

About 16% of youth lacrosse ED injuries were concussions, at a higher annual rate than youth football (443 vs 355 per 100,000 participants); boys' concussions mostly came from hitting the ground, girls' from ball or stick contact (youth, NEISS).

Women's lacrosse injuries come more from ball and stick contact than body contact, with more head/face injuries than in men; ankle injuries dominate in female youth; attackers are injured most and goalies least (review).
Boys' lacrosse is the second-highest male sport for per-season ACL risk after football (0.64% per season) in adolescents.

differences.finding: Midfielders run fastest and sprint most and were injured most in boys' club play.
Goalkeepers have the lowest share of injuries in both boys' and women's lacrosse.
In women's lacrosse attackers had the most injuries.

riskReduction.finding: Because girls' lacrosse injuries are disproportionately non-contact and ACL injury is common in female field sports, neuromuscular ACL programmes are the best-supported option (trials mostly in soccer, basketball and handball).
riskReduction.effect: ACL odds about halved; greater in high school-age athletes (OR 0.38)

riskReduction.finding: Headgear in girls' lacrosse is debated: stakeholders saw possible head/face benefit but worried about more aggressive play; no effect size available from this source.

warmup.finding: No lacrosse-specific warm-up trial found; youth team-sport neuromuscular warm-ups reduce lower-extremity injuries by about a third.

adolescent.finding: Concussion rates in youth lacrosse rose over 2006-2019 as participation grew.
Club sport participation increased ACL injury risk in adolescents roughly 4-fold per exposure.

demands.finding: In pro men's field hockey, 1-minute peak periods far exceed match averages; forwards had the highest player load per minute and defenders the lowest running and heart-rate demands but similar accelerations and decelerations (pro).

In elite women's field hockey, forwards had the highest peak high-speed running in the most intense minute compared with defenders and midfielders; training should prepare players for peak, not average, intensity (elite female).
Field hockey, like most team sports, has more high-intensity decelerations than accelerations in match play (systematic review).

injuries.finding: Most field hockey injuries are minor and ankle sprains are the commonest; men have more and more severe injuries; severe injuries are to the head, face and upper limb from stick or ball contact (review).
Lifetime prevalence of mouth and tooth injury was 20-29% among Dutch and international players even though most wore mouthguards; current mouthguards may not give enough protection (cross-sectional).
In amateur field hockey, collisions, ball and stick caused shoulder, neck, head and face injuries, and few were diagnosed as concussion, suggesting under-recognition (amateur survey).
In team sports including field hockey, female players have about twice the ACL injury rate of males (meta-regression).

differences.finding: Forwards reach the highest peak player load and high-speed running.
Defenders have lower running demands but similar acceleration/deceleration counts.

riskReduction.finding: Balance training, alone or in a programme, reduced ankle injuries by 36-42% (soccer data; ankle sprain is the commonest field hockey injury, so this is a reasonable transfer).
Neuromuscular ACL programmes roughly halve ACL injury in young female athletes, most so in middle and high school.
riskReduction.dose: about 24 min, about 2.5 times per week, about 18 h total

riskReduction.finding: Face and hand protection and mouthguards are commonly recommended because severe injuries come from stick and ball, but mouthguard protection appears incomplete.

warmup.finding: FIFA 11+ style structured warm-ups reduced overall injuries by about 39% in soccer; no field-hockey-specific trial was found here.

adolescent.finding: Female adolescents have about 1.4-1.6 times the ACL risk of male adolescents overall, and ACL injuries are far more frequent in games than practice.

demands.finding: Cheer has evolved into a year-round, acrobatic sport of stunts, tossing and tumbling with high athletic demands (AAP policy).

Dancers are performing athletes whose training is often skill-focused; in adolescent ballet, boys' jump height rose with training year while girls' did not and girls became more injury-prone with age, possibly because of a ballet-only training approach without supplementary conditioning (adolescent ballet).

injuries.finding: Overall cheer injury rate is fairly low but time lost after injury is long; cheer accounted for about 66% of catastrophic injuries in high school girl athletes over 25 years (AAP).
Cheer ED injuries fell 15% from 2010 to 2019 and stunt injuries fell, but concussions and closed head injuries rose 44% and hospital admissions rose (age 5-25, NEISS).

In ED data, cheer injuries were mostly sprains/strains (44%), fractures (17%) and contusions; the commonest mechanism was collision between cheerleaders (29%), then stunting (20%) and tumbling (11%) (NEISS, mean age 14.6).

Catastrophic cheer injuries in high school and college occurred at about 2.1 per million cheerleaders, mostly in practice, to the head (52%) and cervical spine (32%); basket tosses were the leading cause (high school and college).
Collegiate cheer injury rates were 2.4-2.8 per 1000 exposures, mostly sprains/strains, concussions and fractures, with stunting and practice as the main contexts (systematic review).
In a high school cheer survey, 41% had an injury in the past year; the ankle (24%), back (16%) and wrist/hand (16%) were most affected (high school).
Dance students and teachers injure at about 0.8-4.7 per 1000 dance-hours, similar to professional dancers, mostly overuse injuries of the lower limb (systematic review).

Pre-professional dancers in a 30-week prospective study had 5.5 injuries per 1000 hours; knees, lower back, feet and groin were the main sites, with higher rates in females; adolescents had more moderate-to-severe injuries than university dancers.
Youth street dancers (median age 16) had about 4.5 injuries per 1000 dance-hours, mostly acute knee injuries during breaking (youth).

differences.finding: Stunting and tossing roles (basket tosses, pyramids) drive catastrophic head and neck injury; collisions between cheerleaders are the commonest overall mechanism; ankles and wrists bear load in tosses and braces.
Ballet and contemporary injuries are mostly overuse in the lower limb; street dance and breaking have more acute knee injuries.

riskReduction.finding: Banning basket tosses on hard surfaces cut the catastrophic basket-toss injury rate nearly 4-fold (1.55 to 0.40 per million).
Cheer risk factors include higher BMI, previous injury, hard surfaces, stunting and poorly trained coaches; recommendations include coach certification, proper matting and spotting.
Lower strength may be linked to injury in pre-professional ballet dancers, but evidence is too weak to design a proven prevention programme yet.
Excessive compensated and functional turnout range was greater in injured dancers and may help screening.
A cheer review recommends closed-chain eccentric strength work and technique work alongside rule changes, though trial evidence is thin.

warmup.finding: No cheer or dance structured warm-up trial was found in this search; the youth neuromuscular training evidence is the nearest guide.

adolescent.finding: Cheer participants are mostly girls aged 6-17; children aged 5-11 have a higher share of moderate-to-severe cheer injuries than teens.
Adolescent dance and gymnastics ED injuries in girls are mostly strains/sprains and fractures.

findings.finding: In high school athletes across sports, each extra pound of overall neck strength was linked to 5% lower odds of concussion, after adjusting for sex and sport (high school, 51 schools).

Resistance training clearly increases isometric neck strength (large effect, SMD 0.85, high-quality evidence), but no trial has yet tested whether it lowers concussion incidence, and it did not clearly change head acceleration (systematic review and meta-analysis).
A 2026 meta-analysis of five studies found no statistically significant neck-strength difference between concussed and non-concussed athletes; the link remains inconclusive.
In male rugby, cervical strengthening reduced concussions by about 45% (two studies); no evidence yet for females.
In adults, neck strengthening improved isometric neck strength but no study showed fewer cervical spine injuries (systematic review, three studies).

Neck training programmes using isometric or dynamic resistance generally increase strength, with smaller gains at low intensity or frequency; isometric training was linked to fewer match cervical injuries in pro rugby union (review).
Isometric neck strength, but not neck size, appears to predict lower concussion risk; optimal dose is unknown (review).
Neuromuscular warm-ups showed a non-significant trend toward fewer concussions overall (RR 0.69), while rugby movement-control programmes reported up to 60% lower concussion rates.
In collision sports, the tackle causes most shoulder injuries (50-85%), with Bankart lesions, SLAP tears, dislocation and rotator cuff tears common (systematic review).
Male sex, younger age at first dislocation and contact sport participation raise recurrence risk; non-operative care allows same-season return but with high recurrence (review).
High school football players returning after stabilisation surgery had about a 17% recurrence, higher with more seasons remaining.

Shoulder injury mechanisms in rugby (falling on an adducted, internally rotated arm; direct lateral blow) suggest training safe falling, tackle technique and shoulder strength, though no collision-sport shoulder prevention trial was returned by this search.
Youth neuromuscular training programmes reduced lower-extremity injuries by 36% (IRR 0.64) and showed a non-significant reduction in knee injury (meta-analysis of RCTs).
ACL prevention programmes halve all ACL injuries and cut non-contact ACL injuries by two-thirds in females; data for males alone are insufficient (meta-analysis of meta-analyses).

In young female athletes neuromuscular training reduced ACL risk from 1 in 54 to 1 in 111; average dose was about 24 minutes, about 2.5 times per week, about 18 hours total; landing stabilisation and lower-body strength exercises in every session improved the effect, and school-age athletes benefited most.
FIFA 11+ reduced overall injury by 39% (IRR 0.61) in recreational and sub-elite soccer, while the older FIFA 11 did not (meta-analysis).
Balance exercises alone reduced ankle injuries by 42% and balance-containing programmes by 36% (soccer meta-analysis).
Programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise reduce hamstring injuries by about half across sports (risk ratio 0.49).
A simple adductor strengthening programme reduced the prevalence of groin problems in male soccer players by 41% (cluster RCT).

The Copenhagen adduction exercise reliably increases adduction strength, with gains depending on repetitions done, but isolated use did not significantly reduce groin injury (very low-quality evidence).

crossCutting.topic: Adolescent athletes: resistance training, growth and specialisation

findings.finding: Supervised youth resistance training is endorsed as safe and beneficial by an international consensus and by the NSCA position statement.
Resistance training in at-risk youth (early specialisers, inactive youth, girls) has been reported to reduce injury risk by up to 68%.

Injury incidence and burden generally rise with maturity; growth-related injuries peak around the adolescent growth spurt, and faster growth in height and leg length is linked to more injury (elite youth, scoping review).
Higher degrees of sport specialisation are likely linked to overuse and lower-extremity injury; sports-medicine bodies recommend multisport participation (review).
Specialised youth athletes are more injury-prone, though few studies separate specialisation from training volume; delaying specialisation until at least adolescence is advised.
Overuse, overtraining and burnout come from loads exceeding recovery; burnout is a main reason youth leave sport (AAP clinical report).
Female team-sport athletes have about 2.2 times the ACL injury rate of males, but males have more upper-limb, hip/groin and thigh injuries (meta-regression).
